newsitem.title: POLAND: Hungarian high leads E.Europe bourses this week.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian high leads E.Europe bourses this week.

text.p: An optimistic earnings outlook for Hungarian firms helped the Budapest bourse post an all-time high this week while Czech stocks inched up and Warsaw fell due to a heavy primary market.
Elsewhere, Croatian shares rose and the Romanian indexes hit year highs, but other regional bourses saw losses.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which follows price movements in 72 Hungarian, Polish, Czech, Slovak and Slovenian shares, remained virtually unchanged. @
BUDAPEST

Hungarian shares hit an all-time high on Wednesday but though profit-taking trimmed some of the gains on Thursday and further corrections were likely, traders said the longer-term outlook remained positive thanks to strong earnings.

"It (the market) remains fairly well supported," said Roger Monson, chief equity strategist at Daiwa Europe Ltd. "I wouldn't expect a large correction even if you have some sort of weakness in nearby markets in Prague or Warsaw," he added. @
PRAGUE
Czech shares edged slightly higher in the week to Thursday but volume was thin.
The highlight of the week was the return of SPT Telecom, the most heavily weighted Czech share, accounting for 19.7 percent of the offical PX50 index's capitalisation.
SPT had been suspended ahead of its annual general meeting and its return heralded a pick-up in overall market activity as well as solid gains for the issue.
"Recently, I've read a series of surveys from recognised brokerage firms...and everyone says that people should be overweight on Telecom," said Radek Vavra of Citicorp Securities.
WARSAW
Polish shares fell 2.9 percent this week to 15,996.9 points after last week's gain and analysts said the market was locked in its three-month horizontal trend amid conflicting signals.

Analysts said May earnings data released this week were mediocre but that optimism over Wednesday's news that the privatisation offer of large Bank Handlowy was heavily oversubscribed cheered the market.

"The oversubscription is a good sign, it shows interest in big Polish firms, seen by today's (Thursday's) outperformance by the WIG 20 (large-cap index)," said Bogdan Kornacki, a trader at Wielkopolski Bank Kredytowy (WBK) brokerage.

Analysts said much of the money mobilised in the Handlowy oversubscription could go to the public offering of copper giant KGHM Polska Miedz SA starting in late June, though enough should go to stocks to prevent steep falls by the main index. @
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks continued to gain through the week, seemingly buoyed by Franjo Tudjman's victory in presidential polls, and traders saw a sustained uptrend next week.
Blue chip drug maker Pliva stole the show, rising continually on large volumes to touch 501 kuna on Thursday ahead of its annual meeting.
Zagrebacka Banka's ordinaries held firm at 2,035 kuna earlier in the week but were not traded on Thursday.
Chocolate maker Kras and Karlovacka Pivovara brewery also benefitted from stronger investor interest, rising to 445 and 405 kuna respectively. But Podravka lost steam and receeded to 283 kuna.
BUCHAREST
Most Romanian shares gained this week but falling volumes suggested a correction next week, traders said.
Three independent market indices climbed to new year highs.
The CAS-SE index, launched by Romania-based Creditanstalt Securities, was launched this week and rose 24.22 percent. @
BRATISLAVA
Slovak shares fell in listless trade this week with brokers expecting no significant improvement in the medium term.
The 16-share SAX index fell 6.09 points, or 3.44 percent, to close at a new year-low of 170.85 points on Thursday.
"There are no domestic players on the market at the moment, and the foreign investors are cautious over the possibility of a devaluation of the crown," Libor Briska of Creditanstalt said.
The BSE has been in decline since the country's money market was paralysed by foreign speculation in April and May. @
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares fell 2.82 percent this week as the blue-chip SBI index fell 34.83 points to 1,200.8. Turnover rose to 266.7 million tolars ($1.7 million) from 235.7 million.

"I expect shares to fall gradually on poor volumes over the summer -- activity would be boosted by any news about EU treaty ratification. In a matter of a few days after the news the index could move up or down by 10 percent," said Goran Brankovic, a trader of Nova Ljubljanska Banka.

Two weeks ago the constitutional court delayed the ratification of the treaty, which was signed in June last year, and ordered parliament to change the country's constitution in order to allow foreigners to own real-estate.
